source_metadata.title: Implementation of a Best Practice Advisory-Based HIV Screening Program in the Emergency Department with Integrated Infectious Diseases: A Descriptive Study
source_metadata.setting: single urban emergency department in Detroit, Michigan

source_inconsistencies.location: Results narrative page 5 vs Table 4 pages 12-13
source_inconsistencies.issue: The Results narrative reports 51/77 (67.8%) at 3 months and 45/70 (71.1%) at 6 months, while Table 4 reports 51/77 (66.2%) and 45/70 (64.3%). The table percentages match the stated numerators and denominators; both source representations are preserved as separate atoms rather than silently reconciled.
Twelve-month viral suppression is reported as 54/74 (72.9%) in narrative text and 54/74 (73.0%) in Table 4, consistent with a rounding difference.

extraction_limitations: No study details were invented when not reported.
The source is an accepted manuscript and may differ from the final version of record.

Figure 1 was visually inspected to confirm the BPA workflow; atomization prioritizes independently reviewable textual/process assertions rather than reconstructing every role-specific box in the figure.
Claims in the Discussion and Conclusion that attribute linkage success to ED-ID collaboration are represented as author conclusions rather than converted into causal reported results.
All atoms are marked needs_review because extraction was performed by a language model and has not been human verified.

atoms.canonical_statement: The study aimed to describe the ED BPA-driven HIV screening system and evaluate linkage-to-care outcomes among patients with newly diagnosed HIV, while also describing demographic, testing-indication, and clinical characteristics.

The study was a retrospective observational medical chart review conducted after implementation of a BPA-based HIV screening system in a single urban Detroit emergency department with approximately 95,000 annual visits.
Medical records from November 2019 through October 2025 were extracted.

All patients with newly diagnosed HIV infection during the study period were included regardless of whether ED testing was prompted by the BPA or by pregnancy, STI diagnosis, opportunistic infection, or other high-risk features.

population.label: Patients with newly diagnosed HIV infection during November 2019-October 2025
inclusion_criteria: New HIV diagnosis during the study period

atoms.canonical_statement: The BPA prompted a fourth-generation HIV test for ED patients aged 18-65 years who had a CBC performed, no documented HIV history, and no prior HIV test in the current EMR.

concept.text: BPA-based fourth-generation HIV screening prompt

exposures.details: Triggered in the ED for age 18-65 years, CBC performed, no documented HIV history, and no prior HIV test in the current EMR.

atoms.canonical_statement: After an HIV test was ordered, nurses were prompted to inform the patient about testing and offer an opportunity to decline.
A positive HIV screening result automatically underwent confirmatory testing with an HIV differentiation assay.
For a positive confirmatory test, the ID nurse discussed the diagnosis, provided counseling, scheduled the first ID appointment, and involved social work when needed to address barriers to care.
Patients who could not be contacted were referred to Michigan Department of Health and Human Services disease intervention specialists for additional outreach.
The chart review extracted demographics, comorbid conditions, prior and current STI diagnoses, reason for ED HIV testing, and HIV testing history from the EMR.
One ID physician performed chart abstraction using an electronic data-entry form, and a second abstractor reviewed 30% of charts.

A diagnosis was classified as BPA-only when chart review found that the ED provider was not already considering an STI, opportunistic infection, high-risk feature, or pregnancy in medical decision-making.
Linkage to care was defined as attendance at the first appointment with an infectious diseases specialist after a new HIV diagnosis.

concept.text: Linkage to HIV medical care

outcome.definition: Attendance at the first appointment with an ID specialist after a new HIV diagnosis

atoms.canonical_statement: Viral suppression was defined as HIV-1 RNA below 30 copies/mL, with post-treatment time points assessed at 3, 6, and 12 months.

concept.text: Viral suppression

atoms.canonical_statement: Patients without Henry Ford documentation of a post-diagnostic ID visit, ART initiation, or viral-suppression testing were treated as missing for the relevant outcome analyses and excluded from those analyses.

Annual HIV positivity was calculated as new HIV-1 diagnoses divided by HIV tests performed each year; year-specific positivity was compared with 2020 using log-link Poisson models with a test-count offset and robust standard errors, two-sided p<0.05, and no multiple-comparison adjustment.
During 2019-2025, 75,914 ED patients were screened and 176 were newly diagnosed with HIV, for an overall new test positivity rate of 0.232%.

atoms.canonical_statement: Because the study was retrospective and based on ED screening, the diagnosed cohort may not reflect the overall demographics of the HIV epidemic.
The study could not reliably assess why providers opted out of BPA testing and had no data on characteristics of patients who declined HIV testing.
Linkage-to-care, viral-load suppression, and CD4 trends were unavailable for patients who obtained medical care outside the Henry Ford Health system.
Seventy-two patients lacked documented clinic-appointment attendance, and the study could not determine whether they received care elsewhere or did not pursue follow-up.
ART initiation was delayed for some hospitalized patients with opportunistic infections such as cryptococcal meningitis, which increased the median time to ART initiation.
The data-collection period overlapped the COVID-19 pandemic, which may have negatively affected linkage-to-care efforts because of staffing challenges.
Because pre-implementation linkage data were unavailable, the study could not formally assess the association between ED-ID collaboration and linkage to care.

The authors conclude that an automated non-targeted opt-out ED HIV screening program with integrated ED-ID collaboration may be a valuable and feasible model for identifying previously undiagnosed HIV and reducing missed diagnostic opportunities.

The authors conclude that ED-ID collaboration is essential for facilitating linkage to care and rapid ART initiation, which they state promotes viral suppression, improves patient outcomes, and reduces ongoing HIV transmission.
The authors reported that no funding was provided for the study.

The study data came from electronic medical records and are not publicly available because of potentially identifiable information and institutional privacy rules; de-identified data may be available from the corresponding author on reasonable request.
